book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits

chapters.relation: Reads the Deckard-Rachael sex scene in Do Androids Dream and the unfilmed Hampton/Fancher script, where Rachael says 'don't think about it, just do it,' to argue that the felt intensity of passion makes the real/simulated distinction pointless whenever behavior is indistinguishable. The Voight-Kampff test is presented as a version of the Turing Test, grounded in positivism's view that unverifiable inner consciousness is a meaningless question, with supervisor Bryant's 'skin jobs' sneer voicing the objection that passing behavior may be mere rule-following.

chapters.file: ch57 -  . . You Ever Take That Test Yourself.md
chapters.relation: Rachael's question to Deckard at the piano ('you ever take that test yourself?') and Luba Luft's suggestion that a human Deckard was killed and replaced put the viewer in the same quandary about implanted memories. The Penfield mood organ lets humans dial numbered moods, so the empathy that supposedly separates humans from androids is itself artificially inducible, while Phil Resch's torment over whether he is an android — compared to Munch's 'The Scream' — shows the human/android line collapsing from inside.

chapters.file: ch58 - I Love You, My Artificial Construct.md
chapters.relation: Deckard registers an empathic 4.0 on the Voight-Kampff at the thought of retiring Luba Luft, and Resch's remark that including androids in our empathic range would leave us defenseless leads the chapter to Foucault's claim that true/real distinctions reduce to struggles for power. Bounty hunting is read as a reactionary humanism whose 'barrier' keeps humans and androids distinct because technology has otherwise made them indistinguishable — as Deckard's electric sheep, needing exactly the same care as the real one, and the electric toad ('the electric things have their lives, too') confirm.

chapters.file: ch59 -  . . Because My Furnace Believed the House Was Cold.md
chapters.relation: Explains Dennett's physical, design, and intentional stances through a disk drive 'reading' a disk and a thermostat we would never say 'believes' the room is cold, concluding that whether behavior counts as conscious is a choice of vocabulary, not a metaphysical difference. Dick's post-war world of convincing simulacra and economic necessity is the setting in which linguistic conventions shift, explaining Deckard's changed attitudes toward Luba Luft and Rachael.

Applies Searle's Chinese Room to argue that functional equivalence alone would not make androids sentient, then observes that Dick's androids — biological 'chitinous reflex machines' detectable only by bone-marrow and Boneli reflex-arc tests, unlike obviously mechanical electric sheep — may possess the biological 'right stuff' Searle requires for intentional content. It closes by weighing this against the Turing/Dick behavioral view and the Wittgensteinian choice of which language game to play, calling the latter 'the most humanistic' reading.

chapters.file: ch63 - Chapter 09 - Matt Damon Is a Vast Sinister Conspiracy.md
chapters.relation: Argues that 'Matt Damon' is an industrially manufactured person — a simulacrum sustained by executives, marketers, and gossip media that exploits instincts once used to judge trustworthy tribemates. Reading David Norris's tie-choosing specialists in The Adjustment Bureau, Tyrell's 'More human than human,' and the novels The Simulacra and Time Out of Joint, it claims Dick's paranoid fantasy is true: manufactured fake realities keep us docile, distracted, and consuming so we never notice we would rather be lying on a rock in the warm sun.

chapters.file: ch64 - A Variety of Free Will Worth Having.md
chapters.relation: Takes Dick's self-description as a 'fictionalizing philosopher' and reads 'Adjustment Team' — Ed Fletcher stumbling into a world of grey dust animated by an external hidden force — as determinism as we concretely live it: working toward goals we never chose in jobs that are not our own. Thompson's toothpaste line in The Adjustment Bureau becomes the image of consumption-only freedom, while Norris choosing love and politics over the Bureau's plan dramatizes freedom as accepting responsibility for one's own values.

Quotes Dick's A Scanner Darkly author's note — drug misuse 'is a decision,' and the druggie life-style is 'no different from your life-style... only faster' — to argue that dropping out of the plan continues the Sixties' questioning of war, segregation, and monogamy. Dick's refusal of bourgeois moralizing exposes it as part of the social-determinist control system, but a morally neutral natural cause-and-effect is what actually destroyed the druggies, so being free requires taking control, not merely rejecting control.

Frames 'Minority Report' with Nietzsche's charge that men were considered 'free' only so they could be judged and punished, and with Anselm's De Concordia, where God, outside time, foreknows our choices without determining them. Pre-Crime can punish Anderton and the pre-criminals now only because their not-yet-made choices are treated as absolutely free, and the 1954 context — HUAC, Hoover's anonymous accusations, the Communist Control Act — shows people punished for the present guilt of a future crime.

Updates the McCarthyite stakes of pre-guilt with Michelle Bachmann's 'anti-American' probing and the Guantánamo detainees who are 'too dangerous to transfer but not feasible for prosecution.' Dick's own post-2-3-74 spiral — after the pink light he was writing in his Exegesis about telepathic crab-clawed invaders from Sirius — becomes the case study for the book's closing practical problem: how to free yourself from received social, political, and religious determination without careering into drugs, isolation, or madness.

chapters.file: ch68 - Chapter 10 - How to Build a Democracy that Doesn’t Fall Apart Two Hundred Years Later.md

chapters.relation: Updates Plato's rule of the wise to the pre-cogs of 'Minority Report,' noting that Socrates' 'divine sign' made him a kind of pre-cog. It then argues expertise cannot be operationalized — self-proclaimed authorities from Sarah Palin to Barack Obama disagree, and there is no accepted test of who the experts are — closing with Plato's own comparison of voters to children choosing between the doctor's medicine and the confectioner's candy, which explains why the Founders added the Electoral College.

Sets Solar Lottery's Bottle beside the Athenian kleroterion and Madison's fear of factions: because telepaths make any strategy predictable, the Bottle game is a pure game of chance like dice rather than poker. The random twitch that deposes Reese Verrick for Leon Cartwright illustrates the same logic behind Philips and Callenbach's A Citizen Legislature proposal to replace the House with a randomly selected 'portrait of the people in miniature.'

Uses Joseph Schumpeter's deflationary account of elections — no meaningful popular will, just marketplace competition ensuring rotation in office — to explain Herb Moore's claim in Solar Lottery that the Bottle's random twitch prevents dictators. Since no one can be sure of holding power, a lottery guarantees turnover at least as well as elections, though it introduces the mirror-image danger of simply selecting an incompetent.

Walks through Solar Lottery's two-part selection machinery — the random Bottle plus the Challenge, an officially appointed assassin who filters out incompetent Quizmasters like the psychotic Robin Pitt — comparing them to Athenian scrutiny of officials and impeachment. It also shows how the unk underclass selling its power cards concentrates any chance of office in the hands of the rich, undercutting the lottery's democratic justification, and asks whether surviving assassination predicts governing any better than winning elections does.

chapters.file: ch73 - How Can Random Machinery Be Rational.md
chapters.relation: Answers Verrick's complaint that the Bottle is irrational by distinguishing tools, which are arational, from agents who act for reasons: a lottery is inappropriate for choosing a spouse or career but rational where unpredictability or impartiality is wanted. In Solar Lottery the assassins DeFalla and Keith Pellig randomize their courses against telepaths, just as draft and green-card lotteries ensure equal chances, so random rotation in office is a rational tool for stopping anyone from holding power too long.

Takes Plato's warning that those who want to rule, like Verrick, will profit from office — true philosophers rule only under compulsion — into the question of whether power cards may be given away or sold. Since we permit donating organs and having sex but criminalize selling them, letting the rich buy up the unks' tickets destroys the equal-chance rationale, the realization that leads Cartwright to see the game as stacked, and that the chapter links to Lani Guinier's smeared electoral-reform proposals.

chapters.file: ch75 - Chapter 11 - We Can Manipulate You Wholesale.md
chapters.relation: Reads Total Recall's opening scenes — Harry's shifty eyes, then the reveal that his friendship, Lori's marriage, and even Benny's cab-driving are all sanctioned deceptions directed at Quaid — as manipulation commissioned by an outside element that sets the agenda of each relationship. Using people this way already troubles Kantian ethics, the chapter concludes, and an outside element directing individuals to do it is 'potentially enough to have Immanuel Kant spin in his grave.'

chapters.file: ch76 - Sure I Deceived You, but What about Me.md
chapters.relation: Classifies Bob Arctor's undercover drug enforcement, Quail's covert action in 'We Can Remember It for You Wholesale,' and Quaid's HUMINT work as species of spying — one party manipulating or dominating another, as James McCargar's secret-war tradecraft describes. It asks how manipulation is actually done, answering that the manipulator finds weaknesses and links desired behaviors to them, and turns the moral question back on the deceivers themselves.

chapters.file: ch77 - Finding a Lever for Manipulation.md
chapters.relation: Explains the spy tradecraft acronym MISE (Money, Ideology, Sex, Ego) and walks through 'Fred's' recruitment method in A Scanner Darkly — building trust through drug purchases under false pretenses until the mark must betray another confidant for Fred's benefit. The same template covers Lori, Harry, and Hauser in Total Recall, for whom Quaid 'becomes nothing more than a means': monitoring his return to Mars, or locating the rebel leadership.

chapters.file: ch78 - Categorically, We Have an Imperative Problem.md
chapters.relation: Measures the spying in A Scanner Darkly and Total Recall against Kant's second formulation of the categorical imperative: Benny merely tracks Quaid, while the federal agents sacrifice 'Fred's' entire psyche, devaluing his humanity as a mere means. It then stages the real-world debate the fiction mirrors — the Pike and Church Committees, Godfrey's preference for technological collection, and Langan's utilitarian defense that devaluing a few is justified when society's safety requires it.

chapters.file: ch79 - Utilitarian Doesn’t Necessarily Mean Coveralls.md
chapters.relation: Lays out the utilitarian case for the spying in A Scanner Darkly: with New Path immune to inspection and Substance D addiction spreading, sacrificing Bob Arctor — secretly addicted to breakdown point and implanted with the little-flowers trigger — maximizes outcomes for the many. Against this stands the Kantian rebuttal that he should never have been made 'just another means,' likely never again to be 'an able-minded and self-determining person,' and the chapter adds the overlooked victim: the manipulator who violates the categorical imperative.

chapters.file: ch80 - Only Remembered as the Blonde Shot in the Head.md
chapters.relation: Asks whether Total Recall's Lori and Harry — liars, adulterers, willing killers — are immoral people, noting the utilitarian excuse of serving a greater good fails because the Martian government they serve is itself profit-driven and rules by 'the one-way dialogue of the truncheon and rifle.' Following Godfrey, it concludes that an employer who bases jobs on violating individuals' rights will damage the moral frameworks of the employees, whatever their prior calibration.

Extends the moral-damage analysis one level up: organizations develop their own moral personas, and the LAPD's compartmentalization — where 'Fred' may be spying on fellow detectives and is required to lie to his supervisor 'Hank' — normalizes law-breaking in the name of law enforcement. It argues that society's oversight, the intelligence committees created after the Pike and Church hearings, is the 'bullet-proof vest' allowing risky utilitarian spying to continue without corroding everyone involved.

chapters.file: ch82 - Chapter 12 - Grow, My Dears, the Eugenicist Said.md
chapters.relation: Opens the eugenics part with Flow My Tears' Jason Taverner — a beautiful, charismatic, fast-healing 'six' from an abandoned government breeding program, 'not a Nexus-Six, but not unlike one either.' Defining eugenics through the dog-and-wolf contrast in selective breeding, it notes that the 'eu' (good) in eugenics smuggles in an ethical judgment, and poses the part's driving question: who decides what counts as a 'good' or 'bad' trait, and by what right?

Faces the Nazi elephant in the room — the sixes' program terminated in 1943 'politically,' mirroring real eugenics in California — and dismisses reductio ad Hitlerum as fallacious while conceding eugenics' genuinely darker side in Tidman's sterilization bill, which halves the novel's black population each generation. It tests Nicholas Agar's parent-choice 'liberal eugenics' against sex-selective abortions and the widening rich-poor gap, before asking whether bred children should be seen as competitors or as successors to whom we give every opportunity.

Makes the case for eugenics' good side through Jason's uncontroversially desirable traits, invoking Nietzsche's call to 'give birth to a dancing star' and create superhuman successors as a moral philosophy of human improvement. It then probes the limits — beauty is relative (Japan's yaeba), and screening would have lost Van Gogh and Stephen Hawking — before weighing Dick's own compassion for small lives (the electric toad, the avenged cat of 'The Alien Mind,' the potter Mary Anne Dominic) against the blunt statistical claim that healthier, more capable lives go better.

Argues eugenics forces us to discard the 'noble lie' of egalitarian democracy we teach children for their own good, and shows the cost in Jason and Heather's contempt for 'ordinaries,' Jason's aging-obsessed narcissism, and the 'aristocratic values' that let him condemn his lover Heather to a labor camp without qualm. Police general Felix Buckman, demoted for compassion toward labor-camp inmates and later assassinated for criticizing the regime, embodies the democratic values the sixes' elitism destroys, with Marvel's X-Men as the analogy for a fractured next-generation humanity.

Surveys science fiction's next-step humanity — Wells's genetically stratified future, Stapledon's successions of human forms, and the Campbell-era optimism Dick resisted — then turns to contemporary 'posthumanist' theorists like Donna Haraway who want 'human,' 'natural,' and 'gender' fluidly redefined. Dick emerges as the voice of caution in this cross-pollination: expand the definition of what human means, but not at the cost of the compassion and empathy that make us human.

chapters.file: ch88 - Chapter 13 - Things Are Seldom What They Seem.md
ch89 - How Are Things in Glocca Morra—or Anywhere Else, for That Matter.md
chapters.relation: Opens Gerard Casey's part by asking whether David Norris is really free or governed by an external agency, then argues from perception itself: the stick that looks bent in the fish tank and the rainbow that exists only for an observer positioned between sunlight and raindrops show that ordinary experience is already a construct of sensory limits, expectations, and language. This prepares the radical question of whether everything in our experience is in some way an illusion.

Takes Dick's Exegesis self-description ('I am a fictionalizing philosopher') and his twin questions — what is ultimately real, what constitutes the authentic human being — to argue that for Dick the difference between real and fake humans is empathy, not materials. The Adjustment Bureau's emotionally detached bureaucratese ('We are fully licensed to make such corrections') repels, while in 'Human Is' the Rexorian colonizing cruel Lester's body behaves 'more truly human' than the genetic human he replaced.

Traces the 'veil' theme from Parmenides' dokos and the Indian maya to Ed Fletcher seeing 'the fabric of reality split open' in 'Adjustment Team' and the shadow world of 'Jon's World.' It locates Dick's enduring conviction that the empirical world is not ultimately real in the Plato he was given at UC Berkeley — the archetypal realm of Forms behind sensory appearances — and in his professed affinity for Spinoza's Deus sive natura, alongside the Pre-Socratics he devoured.

Reads the Bureau's adjustments as producing alternate realities — Ed Fletcher's boss as 'a different Douglas. A different version!' — and takes déjà vu, Dick's 'manifold of partially actualized realities,' and Ragle Gumm's haunting sense of having been inside a building he has only seen as a model in Time Out of Joint as clues that variables were reprogrammed in our past. Dick's late speculation converges, the chapter notes, with David Lewis's view that possible worlds are as real as ours, and with Hawking and Mlodinow's M-Theory multiverse.

Argues that any theory denying the reality of the ordinary world must presuppose it: the world of mowing lawns, designing experiments, and going for coffee is where all theorizing starts and the world we never leave. The Zen progression — mountains are mountains, then are not, then are again — frames Dick's fake worlds as places we visit so the everyday world can become strange and new to us again, since, as the Hank Williams song has it, we'll never get out of this world alive.

chapters.file: ch94 - Chapter 14 - Trauma of the Real.md
chapters.relation: Introduces Paul Livingston's part with Dick's confession that reading Plato in college convinced him the empirical world was not truly real, then retells the cave of Republic Book VII in detail: prisoners bound since birth watching shadows of puppets cast by a fire. The cave becomes the frame for Dick's fiction — the 'reality' our percept-systems report is a show of images, and the philosophical quest is the prisoner's turn toward the archetypal reality behind the scenes.

Details the disorienting breakthrough in which characters learn that they themselves are fakes: Rachael's distress at her implanted memories ('How can it not know what it is?'), Deckard's paper unicorn in the director's cut confirming his own replicant status, and Ragle Gumm's soft-drink stand dissolving into a slip of paper reading 'SOFT-DRINK STAND' in Time Out of Joint. Each case maps onto the freed cave prisoner's discovery, and the disorientation is pressed onto the viewer: how can I be sure my own life and memories are not a fabrication?

Contrasts Plato, for whom breakdown leads to a deeper and truer reality, with Dick's characters, whose breakthroughs lead only to another shifting reality — then introduces Jacques Lacan's three registers (the Real, the Imaginary, the Symbolic) as the positive account of Dick's 'sense of the real.' For Lacan, ordinary 'reality' — the accountant's respectable job, even the value of money — is purely Symbolic and Imaginary, and 'reality is not Real'; the Real is encountered only when that symbolic order breaks down, as in psychosis.

Uses Dick's 1972 one-sentence definition ('Reality is that which, when you stop believing in it, doesn't go away') and his claim that absolute reality reveals itself only when our space-time categories collapse, arguing the definition fits Lacan's Real better than Plato's picture of looking away from the cave wall. Through Žižek's readings, Ragle Gumm's objects being literally replaced by their symbolic labels and Deckard's replicant recognition as a 'total loss of the hero's symbolic identity' show the traumatic Real first appearing precisely where symbolically constituted reality fails.

Reads Ubik's anti-chronological regressions — rocket to jet to biplane, 1992 decaying into 1939 — through Dick's 'orthogonal time' peeling onion-like layers toward greater Being, which Dick himself compared to Plotinus's concentric emanations from the One beyond all language and comprehension. Dick's 1974 pink-light experience is interpreted as Platonic anamnesis, recovered memory of the forms in a parallel time-stream, shading into the Gnostic conviction that our flawed material universe was created by an imperfect god.

Opens Don Fallis's part with an inventory of Dickian deception: Quaid's implanted memories, replicants deceived into believing they are human in Blade Runner and Impostor, the framed Anderton, Ragle Gumm's manufactured town, and the Bureau's constant adjustments. Unlike Descartes' malicious demon or The Matrix, these are not skeptical hypotheticals but the kinds of deception that corporations, parties, and governments actually perpetrate — with us often complicit in our own deception.

Shifts from the ethics of deception (Kant's near-absolute condemnation of lying versus Plato's morally justified governmental lies) to its epistemology, defining deception as intentionally causing a false belief. This definition explains why Cohaagen deceives Quaid, who falsely believes he is a construction worker, while Rekall cannot deceive the Quaid who really is a secret agent, and why the Zoner Cale merely misleads Spencer Olham in Impostor without deceiving him — with Hume's reasoning about miracle testimony modeling when to believe a probable deceiver.

chapters.file: ch101 - How Do We Get Deceived.md
chapters.relation: Catalogues the channels of deception: the senses (the nonexistent Martian canals, Quaid's fat-lady disguise and hologram watch, and the Adjustment Team literally remaking the world) and, more worrisomely, memory, with implanted pasts for Quaid, Rachael, and the Impostor replicant 'so that the Tyrell Corporation can control them better.' Real cognitive science backs the threat: Nader's reconsolidation experiments show memory is Read-Write rather than Read-Only, and 'lost-in-the-mall' interviews implant rich false memories without any drug at all.

Defines the conspiracy through Cohaagen's team — Lori, Harry, Benny, and the turncoat Hauser — with the Adjustment Bureau as 'the quintessential conspiracy' claiming good consequences for humanity. Popper's argument that belief in efficient grand conspiracies is irrational (his 'cock-up theory of society') is tested against the Bureau's own bungled coffee spill that lets David meet Elise, while Keeley's Hume-style critique and the specter of unbridled skepticism about spouses, friends, and memories frame what it would cost to believe in such conspiracies.

Applies Imre Lakatos's 'degenerating research programs' — geocentric astronomy surviving by adding epicycles — to conspiracy theories like Pentagon 'truthers' who must keep patching their account to explain debris, eyewitnesses, and phone calls. But David Coady's rejoinder, voiced through Lies, Inc. where the 'cranks' who doubted Whale's Mouth were right, and the makeshift excuses for Saddam's WMD, show the official story can be the degenerating program, so rejecting conspiracy theories out of hand leaves you easily manipulated.

Explains Cohaagen's plan — 'Hauser volunteered to become Doug Quaid. It was the only way to fool the psychics' — through Nietzsche's observation that great deceivers are overcome by belief in themselves in the very act of deception, and that one lie obligates twenty more. Against the Impostor replicant and the misled Arctor, the chapter sets the philosophical puzzle that intentional self-deception seems impossible, locating most cases, like Earth's poor clinging to the Whale's Mouth advertisements, in motivated, non-conscious belief maintenance.

chapters.file: ch105 - How Can We Detect Deception.md
chapters.relation: Reads the Voight-Kampff test as a Turing Test variant in which the examiner must catch the machine pretending to be human, noting its everyday descendant CAPTCHA and its inversion of the polygraph: lack of emotion, not stress, is the tell that a subject is not human. Dick's characters mostly detect deception the way we do, by inconsistency — Rachmael ben Applebaum's looping audtrack exposes the Whale's Mouth hoax, and Quaid realizes Edgemar must be lying because a man implanted in a dream would not sweat at the prospect of being shot.

holes.name: Eugenics
holes.what: The deliberate control of human hereditary traits in a population through selective breeding or genetic intervention in pursuit of traits judged 'good'.
holes.why: Chapters 82-86 are built on Flow My Tears' engineered 'sixes' and Tidman's sterilization bill, and no existing taxonomy slug names eugenics itself rather than applied ethics in general.

holes.name: Posthumanism
holes.what: The view that 'human' is a narrow, essentialist notion being superseded, urging fluid redefinitions of the human, the natural, and the gendered (associated with Donna Haraway).
holes.why: Chapter 86 engages posthumanist theory as the contemporary philosophical counterpart to science fiction's next-step humanity and Dick's caution about it, and no taxonomy slug names it.

holes.name: Jacques Lacan
holes.what: French psychoanalyst who divided experience into the Imaginary, the Symbolic, and the unknowable Real, arguing ordinary 'reality' is a symbolic-imaginary construction.
holes.why: Chapters 96-98 interpret Dick's breakthroughs, Deckard's identity loss, and Ubik's regressions through Lacan's three registers and his slogan 'reality is not Real', which the taxonomy cannot tag.

holes.name: The Real (vs the Symbolic and the Imaginary)
holes.what: Lacan's order of what resists all symbolization and imagery, encountered only when the symbolic-imaginary construction of everyday reality breaks down.
holes.why: Chapters 96-98 use the Real as their central lens for Dick's collapsing realities, and neither skepticism nor any existing concept captures it.

holes.name: Imre Lakatos
holes.what: Philosopher of science who refined Popper's falsificationism into the methodology of research programmes, distinguishing progressive from degenerating programmes kept alive by ad hoc modifications.
holes.why: Chapter 103's test for the irrationality of conspiracy theories rests directly on Lakatos's 'degenerating research program', a concept the taxonomy lacks.
